By Mike Allen · Nov 26, 2026

🦃 Gobble, gobble! Happiest Thanksgiving! We're grateful to you for making Axios AM part of your morning, and for helping make this the world's most interesting and consequential breakfast table.

  • 🧤 I'm filing from Scott and Sheri's home in Raleigh. Lots of you know my nephew Evan, our lax player, from White House and Axios events over the past 20+ years. Now young Evan is a Dad: 2-year-old Jack is pioneering the next generation of Allens. I hope you meet sneaky tiger Jack at an Axios shindig soon.

Smart Brevity™ count: 1,691 words ... 6½ mins. Thanks to Noah Bressner for the holiday orchestration. And to Bill Kole for the feast-morning magic.
 
 
1 big thing: Grateful for growth
 

Photo illustration: Lindsey Bailey/Axios. Photo: Library of Congress
 

Each Thanksgiving, Axios Macro's Neil Irwin and Courtenay Brown find five reasons to be thankful about the economy. And there are lots:

1️⃣ The economy is ripping. Wall Street has been reeling amid fears about the AI boom's future. But right now, the U.S. economy is growing fast.

  • It grew at a 4.3% annual rate from July through September, according to revised GDP data, well above the 3.4% first reported.

2️⃣ The productivity revival. After years of lackluster productivity growth, the U.S. economy is getting better at producing more with the same amount of labor.

  • That gives businesses room to raise wages without increasing prices, and lets the economy grow faster without fueling inflation.
  • Labor productivity has grown at a 2.5% annual pace since early 2023, compared with 1.5% from 2005 to 2022, according to San Francisco Fed research.

3️⃣ The entrepreneurship boom. Americans filed more than 5 million applications to start businesses in the first 10 months of the year — the fastest pace on record, according to Census Bureau data.

  • Early signs suggest AI is making it easier to start and run a business without hiring staff.
  • The boom is also evident in data from payments company Stripe. The number of new businesses launching on its platform each week has roughly doubled from a year ago, CEO Patrick Collison said last week — a rate of growth without precedent in Stripe's 15-year history.

4️⃣ Low, low layoffs. A year ago, there was deep angst about the labor market as companies looked to an AI-powered future and the unemployment rate edged up.

  • The unemployment rate has held steady at low levels this year, and layoffs are near all-time lows.
  • The rate at which employers laid off or discharged workers was 1% in September, a tick above the 0.9% low in data that dates to 2001.

5️⃣ America's financial dominance. The U.S. remains at the center of the global financial system, giving American companies an extraordinary ability to raise money to finance growth and innovation.

2. 🩺 Pros and cons of Medicare for All
 

Illustration: Aïda Amer/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

Medicare for All is getting a big boost in attention after the midterms. Here's a primer for your Thanksgiving table arguments, via Axios' Adriel Bettelheim and David Nather:

The boldest idea in health care comes down to one massive tradeoff: Guaranteed coverage for everyone in exchange for an eye-popping price tag and an ultra-messy transition.

  • Why it matters: With huge majorities in both chambers, Democrats can try to force a vote when they're in power, although they're likely to find that not everyone in the party is on board.

Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) — a major supporter of Medicare for All who wrote a book about it — is driving the conversation with an offer to name the plan "TrumpCare."

  • Trump reposted his offer and said he'd meet with El-Sayed, telling the New York Post: "Maybe there's some place in the middle that we could go."

✅ The pros: Medicare for All would replace the nation's fragmented insurance system with universal coverage that's subject to a single standard.

  • In theory, that would eliminate the gaps that left 28 million Americans uninsured last year, according to the most recent CDC figures.
  • The coverage would also be "portable," meaning you'd keep the same arrangement if you change jobs or move to a different state. For life.
  • The basic benefits would also be more generous than most existing public and private insurance plans.

⚠️ The cons: Sticker shock. The projected 10-year cost of implementing a plan is about $47 trillion, per the White House Council of Economic Advisers, which predicts higher taxes, more deficit spending and program cuts.

  • There's also the transition to a new system. Sen. Bernie Sanders' 2017 bill would have ended most existing forms of insurance, including workplace coverage, within four years.
  • How the government would handle continuity of medical care during that time is a big unknown. (El-Sayed supports allowing "additional private insurance through unions or employers" so it's not all wiped out.)
  • Critics predict delays in getting medical tests and treatments.

🥊 Reality check: El-Sayed and Trump will probably meet, and it could end with mutual praise and hopeful vibes. El-Sayed likes to flatter Trump. Trump likes to be flattered.

  • But don't take that as a sign that a deal is imminent. There's pretty much zero common ground, other than calling it TrumpCare. Trump hates Medicare for All.

3. 📚 A Thanksgiving gift
 

Cover: Authors Equity
 

I joyfully file this newsletter 365 days a year — and Axios feels privileged to be able to bring it to you for free. Here's my Thanksgiving ask: I'd be grateful if you'd take two minutes to preorder my best friend and co-founder Jim VandeHei's new book, "You Control YOU," for your family, team and friends.

  • Why it matters: There's so little for our young people that's encouraging & empowering. Jim has a healthy, actionable "anti-doom manual" to help the next generation win in life and at work.

"You Control YOU" reflects Jim's & my shared view of the world, informed by countless generous people who've taught us a better way to live.

  • The book is aimed at high school and college students, as well as 20- and 30-somethings, but is useful for all of us.

🎓 Bonus incentive: Jim and I don't keep a dime from our books. Advances and proceeds go to his family's Zotheka Foundation, where every dollar goes to high school grads who can't otherwise afford college. Jim's wife, Autumn, mentors each of them and helps arrange enviable internships.

  • Take control.

How will oil and energy prices affect GDP growth in 2027?
 
 

The energy headwind that limited growth in 2026 will likely flip in 2027 as prices normalize.

Goldman Sachs Research forecasts Brent at $78 a barrel by the end of 2027, which would turn a 0.5 percentage point drag on global growth into a modest boost.

4. 🌧️ Macy's parade bummer
 
Workers inflate balloons in preparation for the now-postponed Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade yesterday in Manhattan. Photo: Yuki Iwamura/AP

For the first time in its 100-year history, the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been postponed because of weather, Axios' Josephine Walker and Julianna Bragg write.

  • An impending nor'easter forced organizers to push the parade to Saturday.

🥣 Morning chefs, rejoice! Your traditional food-prep soundtrack awaits: NBC will broadcast last year's parade today at 8:30 a.m. in all time zones. The postponed parade will air live at 8:30 a.m. Saturday.

A grounded balloon depicts Goku from Dragon Ball Z. Photo: Bing Guan/Reuters

🎈 The big picture: Macy's was expected to celebrate its centennial parade with a record 100 inflatables.

  • Huge balloons can't fly when sustained winds exceed 23 mph or gusts exceed 34 mph.

Last evening near Central Park, famous balloons — the Pillsbury Doughboy, Snoopy, the Wimpy Kid — looked melancholy, "half-inflated, as if in existential limbo," the N.Y. Times notes.

  • Parade officials have only grounded the giant character balloons once before, in 1971, because of weather.

📺 Between the lines: The parade is one of the few non-sports events that still draws tens of millions of Americans to watch the same thing at the same time.

  • Last year, it drew a record 35.7 million viewers across NBC and Peacock.

5. ⛽ Road trip relief
 
Data: AAA. Chart: Noah Bressner/Axios

U.S. gas prices have dropped about 70¢ a gallon over the past month — giving Thanksgiving drivers a break at the pump today, Axios' Ben Geman writes.

  • AAA says regular gas averages $3.56 today.

🛢️ What's happening: More oil is making its way out of the Middle East, bringing relief to the global market.

  • U.S. demand is also down from the summer, and refiners have switched to cheaper winter blends.

Between the lines: Gas is still 18% more expensive than a year ago, but the recent drop could boost holiday travel and consumer spending, Raymond James analyst Pavel Molchanov said.

6. 📝 Dario's response on free will
 

Via X
 

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei rejected the notion that humans should surrender free will to AI, offering his most definitive view on the question after Axios reported a growing ideological divide among top AI executives.

  • Why it matters: These are Amodei's most significant public remarks since the company went public last week, Axios' Madison Mills writes.

🔬 Zoom in: Amodei said that "we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security."

  • He distinguished between handing over governance to AI, which he opposes, and automating specific tasks, on which he holds more nuanced views.
  • He also said it may make sense to slow or stop certain AI deployments to mitigate job disruption and limit AI's ability to autonomously develop more powerful systems.
  • He took aim at rival AI executives, accusing them of engaging in "vibes-based commercial and political positioning."

🏛️ Mady's original story lit up X yesterday: Top Dems, including ones eyeing 2028, called for new restrictions on AI development. Sens. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii), Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) and Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) pushed for immediate action.

7. 🤖 Thanksgiving sous-chef
 

Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

More Americans are turning to AI for Thanksgiving dinner help, Axios' Avery Lotz writes.

  • Campbell's recent State of the Sides survey found that 27% of U.S. adults who celebrate Thanksgiving have used generative AI for holiday planning or cooking, up from 22% last year.
  • 65% of shoppers say they would like to use AI in some aspect of holiday meal planning, according to the Food Industry Association's holiday shopper trend research.

8. 🏈 1 for the road: NFL holiday drama
 
Aaron Rodgers and Pittsburgh Steelers head coach Mike McCarthy chat before Sunday's game against the Eagles. Photo: Michael Owens/Getty Images

The Pittsburgh Steelers cut future Hall of Famer Aaron Rodgers yesterday after he torched head coach Mike McCarthy on ESPN's "The Pat McAfee Show."

  • The Steelers benched Rodgers, 42, in favor of backup Mason Rudolph ahead of tomorrow's game against Denver — then released him altogether.
  • Rodgers said he learned about the decision while on the phone with teammates.

The four-time NFL MVP painted McCarthy, his longtime coach in Green Bay, as a woefully out-of-touch leader.

  • He said McCarthy arrived late to a quarterback meeting, fell asleep twice and walked out "like nothing happened."
  • Rodgers also said McCarthy ended a halftime meeting by saying "1-2-3, Packers!"
